name: Evelyn Berezin
milestone_by_age_26: Career-defining milestones arrived well after age 26: Teleregister/Reservisor airline reservations work ~1962 (age ~37) and founding Redactron with the Data Secretary word processor in 1969 (age 44). Joined Electronic Computer Corporation as head of logic design in 1951 (age 25–26), but that early hire is career entry rather than a dated public breakthrough product or founding milestone.
early_history_summary: Born 1925 in the Bronx to Belarusian Jewish immigrant parents (father a furrier, mother a seamstress). Earned a physics B.S. from NYU (c. 1945–46) and held an Atomic Energy Commission fellowship. Entered computing in 1951 at Electronic Computer Corporation/Elecom, later designed systems at Teleregister including United Airlines reservations, and founded Redactron in 1969.
family_context_summary: Born to a working-class Belarusian Jewish immigrant family in the Bronx; father Soloman was a furrier and mother Rose a seamstress.
parent_family_domain_summary: No documented parental domain expertise in computing or engineering; parents worked in garment/fur trades.
evidence_summary: Evelyn Berezin (1925–2018) is widely credited with pioneering computerized word processing and early airline reservation systems, but both signature achievements landed after age 26. She joined a Brooklyn computer startup as head of logic design in 1951 at about age 26, then did major Teleregister/Reservisor work in the late 1950s–early 1960s and founded Redactron in 1969 at age 44. Under a strict age-26 material-milestone rule, the fame-defining product and company events are too late.

name: Jeff Atwood
milestone_by_age_26: Stack Overflow launched in 2008 when Atwood was 37–38; Coding Horror began in 2004 at age 33–34. UVA graduation in 1992 (age ~21) is ordinary education, not a material career breakout. No independently dated material milestone at or before age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born December 27, 1970. Graduated University of Virginia in 1992 (environmental science with CS minor). Started the Coding Horror blog in 2004, co-founded Stack Overflow with Joel Spolsky in 2008, left Stack Exchange in 2012, and founded Discourse in 2013.
evidence_summary: Jeff Atwood’s defining public platforms—Coding Horror (2004) and Stack Overflow (2008)—arrived in his thirties. No source-backed founding, product launch, or research breakthrough at age ≤26 was identified.

name: Misty Blowers
milestone_by_age_26: No public birth year found. Documented degrees include a 1995 B.S. (Paper Science), 2003 M.S. Computer Science (Syracuse), and 2009 doctorate; SPIE Early Achievement Award in 2018 and CTO/USMC-related roles are later-career. Without a confirmed birth year and without a dated ≤26 milestone, age-26 eligibility cannot be established.
early_history_summary: Studied at SUNY ESF and Syracuse; worked in pulp mill equipment design for six years after undergrad, then moved into computer science, Air Force Research Laboratory cyber operations, Datalytica, and later senior tech/strategy roles including Marine Corps CTO references and George Mason adjunct teaching on blockchain.
evidence_summary: Misty Blowers has no Wikipedia-listed birth year. Her notable awards and leadership roles are mid/late career relative to a 1995 bachelor’s degree. Eligibility fails on missing birth year and lack of a specific dated milestone at age ≤26.

name: Craig McLuckie
milestone_by_age_26: No public birth year found. Signature milestones—co-creating Kubernetes at Google (~2014), founding Heptio (2016), CNCF leadership, VMware acquisition of Heptio, and later Stacklok—are mid-career achievements. Without birth year, age at those events cannot be verified as ≤26; they almost certainly were not.
early_history_summary: Co-created Kubernetes at Google with Joe Beda and Brendan Burns; product lead roles around Google Compute Engine; left Google after about six years; co-founded Heptio (acquired by VMware); later founded Stacklok as CEO.
evidence_summary: Craig McLuckie is a major cloud-native figure, but no reliable birth date appears in reviewed sources, and Kubernetes/Heptio fame is from the 2010s. Marked age_26_ineligible.

name: Arnd Bergmann
milestone_by_age_26: No public birth year found in reviewed sources. Known as a long-time Linux kernel contributor (ARM SoC maintainer, Linaro) with work spanning many architectures and Y2038/highmem topics. Without birth year, no age-26 milestone can be verified.
early_history_summary: Upstream kernel engineer associated with Linaro (nearly from its start), with prior industry experience cited at places such as IBM; maintains and contributes heavily to ARM and multi-architecture kernel code.
evidence_summary: Arnd Bergmann is a respected kernel maintainer, but public biographical sources do not establish birth year or any dated breakout by age 26.

name: Daniel G. Bobrow
milestone_by_age_26: Signature AI program STUDENT was his 1964 MIT PhD thesis under Marvin Minsky, when he was 28–29 (born 29 Nov 1935). Earlier B.S. RPI (1957) and S.M. Harvard (1958) are ordinary education milestones, not material research breakouts by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born New York City 1935. B.S. Rensselaer 1957, S.M. Harvard 1958, PhD MIT 1964 (STUDENT natural-language algebra solver). Later BBN (TENEX), PARC Research Fellow, AAAI president, ACM Software System Award (Interlisp).
family_context_summary: Obituary notes parents Ruth Gureasko Bobrow and Jacob Bobrow; limited further family socioeconomic detail in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Daniel Bobrow’s landmark STUDENT system is firmly dated to his 1964 dissertation (age ~28). No material research product or award by age 26 was identified.

name: Brian Maggi
milestone_by_age_26: No Wikipedia article and no reliable public biography with birth year or dated tech milestone found. Cannot verify any material achievement by age 26.
early_history_summary: Public web presence is sparse and ambiguous across multiple people named Brian Maggi; no clear, source-backed founder/engineer biography with dated milestones was located.
evidence_summary: Insufficient documentation: no confirmed birth year, company founding date, or age-dated breakthrough. Marked age_26_ineligible.

name: Ronald Wayne
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Apple Computer with Jobs and Wozniak on April 1, 1976 at age 41, then sold his 10% stake within weeks. Earlier slot-machine business (1971, age ~37) and Atari documentation work were also after age 26. No material milestone by age 26 found.
early_history_summary: Born Cleveland, May 17, 1934; trained as technical draftsman in NYC. Moved to California 1956. Failed slot-machine venture ~1971. At Atari developed documentation systems; invited as third Apple partner in 1976 at age 41; quickly exited for ~$800.
evidence_summary: Ronald Wayne’s only widely known milestone is Apple’s 1976 founding at age 41. Strict age-26 rule excludes him.

name: Donald Knuth
milestone_by_age_26: In 1960 (age 22), received simultaneous B.S. and M.S. degrees from Case Institute of Technology by special faculty award for exceptional work, and was commissioned to write a commercial ALGOL compiler for the Burroughs B205—launching a path that led to a Caltech Ph.D. and assistant professorship by age 25 (1963).
early_history_summary: Born 1938 in Milwaukee to a Midwestern Lutheran family; father ran a small printing business and taught bookkeeping. At Case Institute he rewrote IBM 650 software, built a novel basketball player-valuation program (1958), and excelled enough to earn dual bachelor’s/master’s degrees in 1960 while writing a Burroughs ALGOL compiler. Ph.D. in mathematics from Caltech in 1963 under Marshall Hall; immediately joined Caltech faculty and accepted the Addison-Wesley commission that became The Art of Computer Programming.
family_context_summary: Raised in Milwaukee in a Midwestern Lutheran German family; father Ervin owned a small printing business and taught bookkeeping, giving modest middle-class stability and exposure to print/precision craft.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father’s printing business provided proximity to typesetting/print craft later relevant to TeX, but not direct computer-science training; no elite tech dynasty documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Case Institute, IBM 650 access, Caltech PhD, Burroughs consulting, prodigy math, printing-family craft
evidence_summary: Donald Knuth’s pre-26 record is unusually well documented: dual Case degrees and a paid ALGOL compiler at 22, Addison-Wesley book commission by 24, and Caltech Ph.D. plus assistant professorship at 25. Early IBM 650 access and competitive mathematical problem-solving (including a famous high-school word contest) show deep prior reps. Family provided stable middle-class support and a printing background, while Case and Caltech supplied elite institutional acceleration. Later Turing Award (1974), TAOCP, and TeX cemented tier-1 status, but the age-26 bar is already cleared by the 1960–1963 sequence.
starting_point: Born 1938 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, to a Midwestern Lutheran German family; father owned a small printing business and taught bookkeeping.
current_position: Professor emeritus of The Art of Computer Programming at Stanford University; living in the Bay Area; continues occasional Computer Musings and TAOCP work.

trajectory.event: Built a statistical player-valuation program for Case’s basketball team that drew national press attention while rewriting IBM 650 system software.
Earned simultaneous B.S. and M.S. from Case by special faculty award and delivered a Burroughs B205 ALGOL compiler under commercial contract.
Accepted Addison-Wesley’s commission to write a compilers book, which expanded into the multi-volume Art of Computer Programming project.
Received Caltech Ph.D. in mathematics (Finite Semifields and Projective Planes) and joined Caltech as assistant professor.
Published Volume 1 of The Art of Computer Programming, establishing the modern analysis-of-algorithms agenda.
Awarded the ACM Turing Award for major contributions to the analysis of algorithms and programming languages.
Released the first versions of TeX, reshaping digital scientific typesetting worldwide.
Became professor emeritus at Stanford after decades as Fletcher Jones / Art of Computer Programming professor.

name: Ken Block (politician)
milestone_by_age_26: Born 1965; Dartmouth CS degree ~1987 (age ~21–22) and early Wall Street/GTECH software jobs through 1991 (age ~25–26) are ordinary early-career employment. Material company outcomes—Kinetic Consulting (1995), Texas debit-card savings work mid-1990s, Simpatico (2001), and Moderate Party founding (2000s)—all occurred after age 26.
early_history_summary: Raised in Milford, Connecticut; Dartmouth College computer science B.S. Wrote trading-desk software in late 1980s; joined GTECH in Providence ~1991; founded Kinetic Consulting (1995–99) and later Simpatico Software Systems (2001). Entered Rhode Island politics via Moderate Party and multiple gubernatorial runs.
evidence_summary: Ken Block’s software entrepreneurship and political profile are well documented after his mid-20s. No specific, independently celebrated product launch or founding by age 26 was found.

name: Bruce Arden
milestone_by_age_26: Major compiler and systems milestones (GAT paper 1959; MAD language ~1959–61; MTS/virtual-memory work in the 1960s) occurred at ages ~32+. Early IBM CPC programming at GM Allison in 1950 (age ~23) and Purdue B.S. 1949 are early career starts, not the material breakthroughs that defined his field impact.
early_history_summary: Born May 29, 1927; Navy radar technician in WWII; Purdue EE B.S. 1949; began computing at GM Allison on IBM CPC in 1950; Michigan computing center leadership; co-authored GAT and MAD; later Princeton EECS chair and Rochester engineering dean. Died December 8, 2021.
evidence_summary: Bruce Arden was a genuine early-computing pioneer, but the dated, field-shaping compiler and OS work sits after age 26. Conservative eligibility fails.

name: Aaron Sittig
milestone_by_age_26: No confirmed public birth year. Early Facebook design work (joined ~2005; photo tagging ~2006; often called Facebook’s first designer) cannot be age-verified as ≤26 without birth date. Whitepages-style age estimates are not sufficient for eligibility.
early_history_summary: Brought into Facebook by Sean Parker; early product/design leadership including friend photo tagging (with Scott Marlette, ~2006) and like-related product work; Design Strategy Lead; left Facebook around 2012. Close to Zuckerberg social circle; later independent design/network work.
evidence_summary: Aaron Sittig’s Facebook design contributions are well known, but missing birth year blocks age-26 verification. Marked age_26_ineligible.
